summary: Introduces "wiretap algorithms", a class of experimental routing algorithms for stations sharing a packet-radio broadcast channel. They compute a primary shortest-distance route plus alternate routes ordered by distance, to use if the primary fails. It is presented as a prototype example that might apply more widely in the Internet.

plainLanguage.summary: If your usual road is blocked, you want a backup road ready. This idea works out the best route and a list of spare routes for radios that share the same airwaves.

subtitle: Computing alternate routes for amateur packet radio using passive monitoring

tldr.problem: Amateur packet radio stations using shared broadcast channels need to find good paths to other stations, avoiding digipeaters when possible and handling hidden stations that cannot hear all traffic.
tldr.mechanism: The Wiretap Algorithm observes paths used by other stations on the channel, builds a database of nodes and links with estimated costs, and computes primary and alternate routes using a shortest-path-first technique similar to that used in the ARPANET.
tldr.outcome: Stations can avoid unnecessary digipeaters, discover new paths, and route around congestion using a simple prototype implementation tested on real packet radio networks in the Washington DC area.

today: RFC 981 describes an experimental prototype from 1986. The approach of passive monitoring to discover routing paths remains relevant to modern wireless networks, though the specific AX.25 radio technology has been superseded by digital modes. The routing principles, particularly computing alternate paths and handling hidden terminals, influenced later wireless routing protocols.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Wiretap Algorithm is a dynamic routing algorithm designed for the AX.25 packet-radio protocol, which allows amateur radio operators to send data on shared broadcast channels at VHF frequencies. The algorithm solves a practical problem: stations on a shared channel cannot always hear all other stations directly (the hidden station problem), and they must choose paths through intermediate stations called digipeaters.

Instead of relying on complex routing protocols or manual path selection, Wiretap uses passive monitoring, listening to frames transmitted on the channel and extracting routing information from the callsigns in the frame headers. This information is used to build a dynamic database and compute both a primary route and several alternate routes to any destination, ordered by estimated quality.

The algorithm is similar in principle to the shortest-path-first algorithm used in the ARPANET, but adapted for the unique constraints of amateur radio: limited computational resources, the need to handle multiple paths, and the presence of hidden stations that affect link quality.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of asking other stations for directions, the Wiretap Algorithm secretly listens to messages passing by, figures out how the network is wired up, and calculates the best path and backup paths to reach anyone on the channel.

sections.title: Design Principles
sections.content:
The Wiretap Algorithm is based on computing link distance, which reflects the probability that a packet will successfully traverse a link. The algorithm assigns weighted factors to each link and node, such as the number of hops, whether the link has been verified by observing traffic in both directions, and whether it carries synchronized data frames. Node factors include the complexity (number of incident links) and congestion level.

A key design principle is that the distance of a path is the sum of weighted factors for each link in the path. This allows the algorithm to compute a set of paths ordered by distance, selecting the one with minimum distance as the primary route and the others as alternates. The algorithm stops if paths exceed a maximum number of hops (eight) or distance (255), preventing infinite loops and bounding computation.
sections.plainLanguage: Each radio link gets a score based on how reliable it seems—direct links score better than ones that go through many digipeaters, and links that have proven to work both ways score better than ones that might be one-way. The algorithm picks the path with the lowest total score, then finds alternatives.

sections.title: Implementation Overview
sections.content:
The implementation runs on an LSI-11 processor using the "fuzzball" operating system, connected to an AX.25 radio interface. The prototype consists of two main routines: the wiretap routine processes monitor headers from the radio and updates the routing database, while the routing routine computes paths when needed.

The database comprises three tables: a node table (one entry per distinct station callsign, indexed by node ID), a link table (one entry per pair of stations with link quality information), and a channel table. Node table entries require 26 bytes each; the implementation maintains about 60 nodes and 100 links under normal operation, with maximum capacities of 75 nodes and 150 links. The algorithm also performs garbage collection using a weighted least-recently-used cache replacement strategy, removing old or low-quality links to make room for new ones.
sections.plainLanguage: The implementation keeps two tables: one listing every station it has heard from and what it learned about how to reach it, and another listing every link between pairs of stations. When the tables get full, it forgets the oldest or least useful information to make room for new observations.

sections.title: Computing Paths
sections.content:
The routing routine uses a variation of the Viterbi Algorithm, building a dynamic list of candidate paths from the destination back to the source. It starts with the destination as the root and iteratively examines each candidate, finding all links that connect to it and adding new candidates to the list. When paths merge at a single node, the algorithm keeps all non-looping paths (unlike Viterbi, which discards lower-ranking duplicates) so that alternate routes are preserved.

Path exploration is pruned using three mechanisms: paths are abandoned if they would create a loop, if the hop count exceeds the minimum hop count plus one (to keep alternates within one extra hop of the best path), or if distance exceeds 255. The prototype averages 5.4 milliseconds to compute one route on an LSI-11/73, or about 3.4 milliseconds when computing both primary and alternate routes.
sections.plainLanguage: The routing routine works backwards from the destination, building a family tree of paths. It prunes away paths that would loop back on themselves and paths that are too long, keeping the shortest one as the primary route and the next-shortest ones as backups.

sections.title: Practical Considerations
sections.content:
In practice, stations often select incorrect or speculative paths, causing the database to accumulate erroneous links. The implementation handles this with age tracking and time-based expiration: speculative links (marked as unverified) expire after fifteen minutes, while other links expire after 24 hours. Age counters are incremented once per minute if below 60, and once per hour thereafter, resetting to zero whenever the link is observed again.

The prototype has been in operation for about four months. Key lessons learned include the value of a finite-state automaton to manage connection attempts with retry logic along alternate routes, the use of heuristic speculative paths (artificially connecting the destination to every digipeater in the database for new stations), and the need for mechanisms to detect failure of transport connections, not just radio links. The implementation also demonstrates the importance of managing processor resources when using spontaneous transitions to implement timers.
sections.plainLanguage: The system learns from experience: if a path was heard from recently, it is considered more reliable; if it has not been heard in a day, it is forgotten. When trying to reach a station for the first time, the algorithm guesses that it might be reachable through any of the known digipeaters and tries them in order.

fields.desc: Bit flags: source, digipeated, heard, synchronized, reciprocal
